pl-l3d6c3-d1e117.summary: Sets out the second opinion: its holders agree partly with the first but say that man consists not only of soul and flesh but of human and divine nature, i.e., three substances: divinity, flesh, and soul, and they call this Christ. There is only one person, simple before the incarnation, but composite of divinity and humanity in the incarnation; not another person than before, but the person of God became also the person of a man, one person of God and man, subsisting in and from two natures. That person is not said to be made a person, though it is said to be made the person of a man; it was made something subsisting of soul and flesh, but not made a person, substance, or nature. As that subsistent it is composite; as the Word, simple.
claims: Christ's person, simple before, became composite of divinity and humanity.
The person of the Word became also the person of a man.
As subsisting in humanity it is composite; as Word, simple.

pl-l3d6c3-d1e120.summary: Cites Augustine in Prosper's Sentences: the Church's sacrifice consists of two things, the visible species of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of Christ, sacrament and reality of the sacrament, just as Christ's person consists of God and man, since each thing contains the nature and truth of the things from which it is made.
claims: Christ's person consists of God and man, as the Eucharist of sign and reality.

pl-l3d6c3-d1e132.summary: Cites John Damascene: in Christ we recognize two natures but one hypostasis composed of both. The Word's hypostasis, simple before, became composite of two perfect natures, deity and humanity, bearing both the characteristic property of divine sonship, which distinguishes it from Father and Spirit, and the characteristic properties of the flesh, which distinguish it from his mother and other men.
claims: Christ's hypostasis, simple before, became composite of two natures.
The one hypostasis bears both divine and human distinguishing properties.

pl-l3d6c3-d1e145.summary: Cites Damascene further: we confess one incarnate hypostasis of the Son in two perfect natures, which remain after the union united in one composite hypostasis. The union is substantial, i.e., real, not imaginary, but it does not make one composite nature; the substantial difference remains: created stays created, uncreated uncreated, mortal mortal, immortal immortal, circumscribed circumscribed, and uncircumscribed uncircumscribed.
claims: The union is real but does not produce one composite nature.
The properties of each nature remain distinct after the union.

pl-l3d6c3-d1e151.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate: as the Father and Son have one nature by deity, so mother and Son have one nature by humanity; from both substances, divinity and humanity, one and the same Jesus Christ is Son of God and man, true God and true man.
claims: Christ is one from two substances.

pl-l3d6c3-d1e163.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate XIII: human nature could be joined to God so that one person was made from two substances, and so from three: God, soul, and flesh.
claims: One person was made from two substances, and so from three.

pl-l3d6c3-d1e172.summary: Sums up: these and other authorities support those who say Christ's person is composed, made, or consists of two natures or three substances.

pl-l3d6c3.summary: Sets out the second opinion, which agrees in part with the first: the man consists not only of soul and flesh but of human and divine nature, three substances (divinity, flesh, soul). There is one person, simple before the incarnation, made composite of divinity and humanity in it; not another person, but the person of God became also the person of a man, subsisting in and from two natures. It is not said to be made a person, though it is made something subsisting of soul and flesh: composite insofar as it is that subsistent, simple insofar as it is the Word. Supporting authorities: Augustine's Sentences of Prosper (the Eucharist and Christ's person both consist of two), John Damascene on one composite hypostasis in two unconfused natures, and Augustine, De Trinitate.
claims: Second opinion: Christ's person, simple before the incarnation, became composite of two natures or three substances.
The person did not become another person, but the person of God became also that of a man.
The two natures remain distinct in the one composite hypostasis.
